guided.title: Unpack a record
guided.prompt: The tuple `row` is `("Ada", 36, "London")`. Unpack it into `name`, `age` and `city`, then print `city`, `name` and `age` in that order on one line separated by spaces.
guided.solution:
row = ("Ada", 36, "London")
name, age, city = row
print(city, name, age)
hints: Put three names on the left of `=` and the tuple on the right.
`name, age, city = row` matches names to items by position.

guided.title: Swap two values
guided.prompt: The variables `low = 90` and `high = 10` are the wrong way round. Swap them without a third variable, then print `low` and `high` on one line.
guided.solution:
low = 90
high = 10
low, high = high, low
print(low, high)
hints: The right side of an assignment is evaluated completely before any name changes.
Write both names on each side, in opposite order.

guided.title: Count the distinct values
guided.prompt: `orders` is `["A1", "B2", "A1", "C3", "B2", "A1"]`. Print the number of distinct order codes, then the distinct codes as a sorted list.
hints: A set keeps each value once.
`sorted(unique)` gives a list, which has a reliable order for printing.

guided.title: Two lists, three questions
guided.prompt: `a = [1, 2, 3, 4]` and `b = [3, 4, 5]`. Print, as sorted lists on three lines: the values in both, the values only in `a`, and all values in either.
guided.solution:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
b = [3, 4, 5]
sa, sb = set(a), set(b)
print(sorted(sa & sb))
print(sorted(sa - sb))
print(sorted(sa | sb))
hints: Turn both lists into sets first.
Intersection is `&`, difference is `-`, union is `|`.
Wrap each result in `sorted()` before printing.

independent.title: Who is new, who left
independent.prompt: `last_week` is `["ann", "bo", "cy", "ann", "di"]` and `this_week` is `["bo", "ed", "di", "fay", "ed"]`. Print three lines: `Returning: ` and the sorted list of people in both weeks; `New: ` and the sorted list present only this week; `Left: ` and the sorted list present only last week. Example format: `Left: ['x']`.
independent.solution:
last_week = ["ann", "bo", "cy", "ann", "di"]
this_week = ["bo", "ed", "di", "fay", "ed"]
last, this = set(last_week), set(this_week)
print("Returning:", sorted(last & this))
print("New:", sorted(this - last))
print("Left:", sorted(last - this))

independent.title: Distinct records
independent.prompt: `rows` is the list `[("Ada", 36), ("Bo", 29), ("Cy", 41), ("Bo", 29)]` of tuples. Print on separate lines: the number of rows; the number of distinct rows (put the tuples in a set); the distinct rows as a sorted list; and then, unpacking the last row of the list into `name` and `age`, the text `name is age` built with `print(name, "is", age)`.
independent.solution:
rows = [("Ada", 36), ("Bo", 29), ("Cy", 41), ("Bo", 29)]
print(len(rows))
unique = set(rows)
print(len(unique))
print(sorted(unique))
name, age = rows[-1]
print(name, "is", age)

independent.title: Head, middle and tail (stretch)
independent.prompt: `values` is `[7, 3, 9, 3, 7, 1]`. Use starred unpacking to put the first value in `head`, the last in `tail` and the middle values in `middle`. Print `head`, `tail`, `middle`, then the middle values without duplicates as a sorted list, and finally whether `head` appears among the middle values (a boolean).
independent.solution:
values = [7, 3, 9, 3, 7, 1]
head, *middle, tail = values
print(head)
print(tail)
print(middle)
print(sorted(set(middle)))
print(head in set(middle))

checks.question: What does `type((5))` return?
checks.explanation: Round brackets alone only group; `(5)` is the integer 5. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`.

checks.question:
What does this print?

```python
items = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]
print(len(set(items)))
```
checks.explanation: The set holds 1, 2 and 3 once each, so its length is 3. The length of the original list would be 5, and `len` returns a number, not a list.

checks.question: Which line creates an empty set?
checks.explanation: `{}` is an empty dictionary, `()` an empty tuple and `[]` an empty list. Only `set()` makes an empty set.

checks.question:
What does this print?

```python
a, *b = (1, 2, 3)
print(b)
```
checks.explanation: A starred name collects the remaining items into a list, so `b` is `[2, 3]`, not a tuple.

checks.question: What does `sorted({1, 2, 3} - {2})` return?
checks.explanation: The difference keeps the items of the left set that are not in the right set: 1 and 3. `sorted` returns a list, so the result is a list rather than a set.
